‍<strong>Le paysage politique municipal: ‍Municipal politics is changing fast. From Villeray to Pointe-Saint-Charles, including Rosemont and Côte-des-Neiges, a number of racialized women candidates from diverse backgrounds are taking their first steps in politics, hoping to lend their voices to the demands of the communities they represent.
<strong>Qu’est-ce qui les a poussées à e: What drove them to embark on this adventure? We talked to four of them.
<strong>‍</strong>La trajectoire de Nafi: ‍Nafija Rahman’s path gradually led her to get involved politically. Curious, in 2017 she took part in a program meant to encourage women from diverse backgrounds to go into politics. A year after that training, which she took through Projet Montréal, then the opposition party, her borough councillor, Sophie Thiébault, let her know she should try her luck in the next election. “Knowing myself, with the headscarf and everything, and what was going on with Bill 21, I knew it would be hard,” admits Nafija Rahman. “As an ally and a mentor, [Sophie Thiébault] managed to convince me that I should try my luck.”
C’est à ce moment que Nafija a fait l’ex: That was when Nafija experienced what she believes is the challenge of being a veiled Muslim woman in politics. “The debate about my headscarf inside Projet Montréal is why it didn’t work out,” she lets slip, dismayed. Raphaëlle Rinfret-Pilon, director general of Projet Montréal, rejects this allegation, however: she says there was a problem with her home address.
L’intérêt pour la politique était tout d: Still, Nafija Rahman’s interest in politics was well and truly awakened. When she saw Balarama Holness launch his own party, she didn’t hesitate to jump in.
« C’était ça, le meilleur choix pour moi: “That was the best choice for me,” she says with a smile. She decided to run as a borough councillor in the Sud-Ouest for Mouvement Montréal.
Pour Ericka Alneus, il est clair que cer: For Ericka Alneus, it is clear that certain “systemic” obstacles are likely to be part of her journey. Nevertheless, having lived in Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie for more than 10 years, she decided that this was the year to enter politics. She explains that she chose this level of government for its “proximity.” “I’m interested in people, and municipal politics lets me maintain that connection and work with the fine hardwood of people,” explains the candidate, who is originally from the Eastern Townships. Ericka has big ambitions for the mandate she is seeking by running for Projet Montréal.
« Je pense qu’on peut changer le système: “I think we can change the system from the inside. I think you have to understand the system to change it, and that’s where my strength lies,” she says in a confident voice. “Maybe [I’ll be able to bring] a different perspective on the system.” She bases her aspirations on her past professional experience.
« J’ai souvent intégré des équipes, prof: “I’ve often joined teams, professionally and on boards of directors, and it’s: ‘OK, what do we do with this? How do we improve it? How do we situate it – for whom and why?’” A graduate in philanthropic management, she is pleased with the plurality of candidates running in this election. “Diversity does justice to the reality in which our societies evolve and grow,” she believes. She starts from the current health crisis to imagine a more inclusive future. “Diversity leads to a better assessment of certain risks or certain issues. [...] I think we deserve to have this diversity that will give us the tools to get through the crises ahead.”
Les élections municipales des 6 et 7 nov: The municipal elections on November 6 and 7 also mark the first steps in politics for Mariem Mathlouthi, a candidate for city councillor in Villeray for the new party Quartiers Montréal. She sees her role in politics as an extension of the one she plays in her neighbourhood as a café owner. “We’re very involved in the community. We make sure that when associations want to hold fundraisers, they turn to us. It’s kind of become a calling for me with regard to the community,” explains the Tunisian-born businesswoman, standing in front of the business she founded three years ago.
Qu’est-ce qui a provoqué le déclic chez: What was the spark that pushed her to go into politics? “I never thought I’d be a politician.
[En parlant avec des gens autour de moi]: [Talking with people around me], I was told: ‘If you’re not interested in politics, you’re the right candidate, because you’ll represent the right things and the real things of the people around you who live in the same community as you.’”
C’est à ce moment qu’elle a décidé de se: That was when she decided to run alongside someone “very frank and down-to-earth,” the mayor of her borough and founder of Quartiers Montréal, Giuliana Fumagalli. Mariem Mathlouthi recalls the impression the mayor made on her at their first meeting. “The first thing I saw was that you can have real people with real empathy who listen to citizens, and they’re politicians on top of that,” she explains. That was all it took to convince her to join the ranks of Quartiers Montréal.
Stéphanie Valenzuela n’a jamais pensé qu: Stéphanie Valenzuela never thought she would run as a candidate in an election. “Growing up, I saw a lot of politicians presenting their platforms, but I never saw politicians who looked like me,” she says right off the bat during our interview. Although she went on to study political science, she simply saw herself working as an advisor and working with elected officials to put policies in place. After her studies, she worked for a humanitarian organization in Mexico for four years.
C’est à son retour à Montréal qu’elle a: It was when she returned to Montréal that she realized that, “yes, it’s important to act at the international level, but there’s a lot of work to do here too, at the local level, in my own community.” So she began a community involvement that has not stopped blossoming since, with organizations in the neighbourhood where she has always lived: Côte-des-Neiges. Over the course of her involvement, she saw people’s needs first-hand. “We’re talking about services, we’re talking about a lack of investment, we’re talking about support [to help young people] at school, to do their homework, to find an apartment in the neighbourhood. When you hear that kind of thing, you ask yourself: ‘What can I do to improve the situation?’” That was all it took for her to join the Ensemble Montréal team and run as city councillor in the Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce borough.
Faisant allusion à ses origines philippi: Alluding to her Filipino roots, she is delighted at the possibility of giving her community a seat at the decision-making table. “We can’t say our opinion isn’t being taken into account if we don’t run. If we don’t take the chance to run, how are we going to be truly integrated into the system, here in Montréal?”
